title: Place n queens on an n-by-n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and count or list all valid placements, using backtracking.
shortTitle: Solve the N-Queens Problem (Backtracking with Constraint Pruning)
keyPoints: Place one queen per row; at each row try every column and backtrack when no column is safe
Constant-time conflict detection uses three sets: occupied columns, row-minus-column, and row-plus-column
Placing a queen adds three constraint keys; backtracking removes them to restore state
The base case (row equals n) means all queens are placed safely and one solution is counted or recorded
The per-row single-queen rule and constraint pruning cut the search far below the naive n^n bound
Board symmetry can nearly halve the first row's work; bitmask encoding speeds up the inner loop
N-Queens is the textbook constraint-satisfaction backtracking problem, the same paradigm behind Sudoku solvers

s1_definition.oneliner: Place one queen per row in a non-conflicting column, tracking used columns and both diagonals, and backtrack when a row has no safe cell.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **N-Queens** – place n chess queens on an n-by-n board so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal.
- **One queen per row** – since each row must have exactly one queen, the decision is which column to choose for each row.
- **Constraint sets** – three sets (columns, row-col diagonals, row+col diagonals) provide O(1) conflict checks.
- **Backtracking** – add three keys on placement, recurse to the next row, remove three keys to try the next column.
- **Base case** – row index equals n means all rows have safe queens; count or record the configuration.
- **Complexity** – super-polynomial but far below n^n due to heavy pruning.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must schedule n critical daily jobs on n servers so that no two jobs clash on the same resource line, where clash rules mirror a queen's reach: same column or either diagonal. A scheduler fills one job per row, skips clashing columns, and backs up whenever a row has no free spot. Every complete non-clashing schedule is one valid solution.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  N-Queens Backtracking (n=4)

  Three constraint sets for O(1) checks:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ cols:  {occupied columns}           │
  │ diag1: {row - col values}           │
  │ diag2: {row + col values}           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Row 0: try cols 0-3, place where sets allow
  Row 1: try cols not in any of three sets
  Row 2: same check
  Row 3: same check -> base case, record

  Solution 1:      Solution 2:
  . Q . .          . . Q .
  . . . Q          Q . . .
  Q . . .          . . . Q
  . . Q .          . Q . .

  Add 3 keys → recurse → remove 3 keys (backtrack)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The N-Queens problem places n queens on an n-by-n board so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal. The single most important insight is that exactly one queen goes in each row, so you just choose a safe column for each row and recurse. Three constraint sets (columns, row-col diagonals, row+col diagonals) make each safety check constant time.

Placing a queen adds three keys to the sets, recursing fills the next row, and backtracking removes the keys. When the row index reaches n, all rows are safely filled and one solution is recorded or counted. The pruning keeps the real search far below n^n, though it remains super-polynomial.

The bitmask optimization replaces the three sets with integers and uses bitwise operations to find free columns in a few instructions, which is much faster for larger n. Symmetry-based pruning nearly halves the first-row exploration.

At the National Bank of India, the constraint scheduler used this paradigm to assign critical jobs to non-conflicting server slots, modeling the clash rules as column and diagonal constraints. N-Queens is the textbook example of constraint-satisfaction backtracking, the same paradigm that powers Sudoku solvers and general CSP engines.

Remember one sentence: one queen per row, three constraint sets for O(1) checks, and backtrack when no column is safe.
